chapter_theme: Nothing lasts: wealth disperses like a theatre crowd, each day is a blade, and life is a lodger in the body. The error is mistaking this for permanence, and the practical conclusion is urgency: do good now.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the error of taking the passing for lasting (331), the impermanence of wealth (332-333), and the impermanence of the body (334-340), which he traces step by step through days passing, death, sudden loss, uncertainty, the corpse, the round of births, and the body not being the soul's own.

331.reading: The paltry understanding that takes what doesn't last for what lasts is the lowest.
331.nuance: The fault is cognitive before it is moral: a mistake of knowledge, sarcastically dignified with ஆண்மை, mastery. Parimelazhagar limits 'lowest' to those seeking release, for whom this error feeds attachment, and the verse doesn't state that limit.

332.reading: The coming of great wealth is like a crowd gathering at a dance hall, and its going is like that crowd breaking up.
332.nuance: A crowd has its own reason for being there, and Parimelazhagar presses this: wealth comes because of good deeds, of its own accord, and leaves when that cause is spent. So the owner is no more than the hall. His addition that this includes heavenly wealth is his own.

333.reading: Wealth has the nature of not staying; if you get it, do straight away what stays.
333.nuance: அற்கா and அற்குப play on one root, so what doesn't stay can be converted into what does. For Parimelazhagar 'what stays' means worship and giving without expecting fruit, leading to release, though the verse doesn't name them.

334.reading: It shows itself as a thing called a day, but it is a blade that saws through life, if one can find those who perceive it.
334.nuance: Parimelazhagar: the fool rejoices that time is passing, and doesn't realize it is his own time. He grammatically dismisses a rival division of the words at length. உணர்வார்ப் பெறின் admits how few will ever see it this way.

335.reading: Before the hiccup rises and stops the tongue, good deeds must be rushed to.
335.nuance: The image is the plain physical detail of the death rattle, with no metaphor. Parimelazhagar notes that it is the tongue being stopped, meaning that one can't even instruct others to act, and that no one knows when it will come.

336.reading: This world has the greatness that one who was here yesterday isn't here today.
336.nuance: பெருமை is bitter here. Parimelazhagar takes it as excess, an overflow of impermanence, while Manakkudavar simply repeats 'greatness'. Kalaignar makes it the world's arrogance, boasting of having killed. All three hear the irony, in different keys.

337.reading: Those who can't know they will live one moment more have thoughts in the many crores.
337.nuance: The disproportion, a moment against crores, is the joke. Parimelazhagar gives a delightful catalogue of what such people plan: acquiring, guarding, overcoming, and raising friends and ruining rivals.

positions.position: The crores are thoughts and schemes.
positions.quote: கோடியளவும் அன்றி அதனினும் பலவாய நினைவுகளை நினையா நிற்பர் அறிவிலாதார்.

positions.position: The crores are what they assume their lifespan to be.

338.reading: The friendship between body and life is like a bird flying off and leaving its குடம்பை alone.
338.nuance: நட்பு, friendship, is heavily ironic: for Parimelazhagar there is none, only a union forced by deeds.

positions.position: குடம்பை is the egg, since a bird grows within it and never returns, and he explicitly rejects 'nest'.
positions.quote: முன் தனியாத முட்டை தனித்துக் கிடப்ப அதனுள் இருந்த புள்ளுப் பருவம் வந்துழிப் பறந்து போன தன்மைத்து,

positions.position: குடம்பை is the nest, and the point is that life leaves whenever it will.
positions.quote: கூடு தனியே கிடக்கப் புள்ளுப் பறந்து போனாற்போலும்;

positions.position: It is the egg and the chick.
positions.quote: உடலுக்கும் உயிருக்கும் உள்ள உறவு முட்டைக்கும் பறவைக் குஞ்சுக்கும் உண்டான உறவு போன்றதுதான்.

339.reading: Death is like falling asleep, and birth is like waking after sleep.
339.nuance: The verse is very short and calm, with nothing about what happens in between. Its tone can be taken as reassuring or as a further turn of the screw. Parimelazhagar says birth is included to show that impermanence is itself what is permanent.

positions.position: Death and birth alternate naturally and quickly, as sleep and waking do.
positions.quote: சாக்காடும் பிறப்பும் இயல்பாய்க் கடிதின் மாறிமாறி வரும்

positions.position: It is a statement of rebirth: the life that went is born again.
There is no cycle: birth is the waking and death is a sleep with no waking.
positions.quote: திரும்ப விழிக்க முடியாத மீளா உறக்கம் கொள்வதே இறப்பு.

340.reading: Has the life that sits as a lodger in the body not found a home of its own?
340.nuance: துச்சில், a lodger's corner in another's house, is homely and sad, and the verse is a soft question rather than a declaration.

positions.position: No body has ever been a permanent home to it, given how life comes and goes among bodies.
positions.quote: எஞ்ஞான்றும் இருப்பதோர் இல் இதுகாறும் அமைந்ததில்லை போலும்!

positions.position: The home is specifically the state of release.
Once it leaves the body, life has no other shelter, which comes close to the reverse.

links.note: 333 says wealth is by nature unstaying; 753 calls it the unfailing lamp that drives out darkness wherever one intends. The chapter on impermanence and the chapter on acquiring wealth describe the same thing in opposite terms.
Both tell the owner of unstable wealth where to put it. 226 names the place: the hunger of the destitute. 333 explains why it must be done immediately.
Both end உணர்வார்ப் பெறின், 'if those who perceive it could be found'. Flesh as a wound, and a day as a blade: in each, the ordinary hides violence, and the verse doubts that many will see it.
36 says not to put off virtue until later, since it is a companion that doesn't die when you die. 335 supplies the concrete deadline: before the hiccup stops the tongue.
340 asks gently whether the lodger has no home of its own. 345 draws the conclusion for one who wants to leave for good: even the lodging is too much, let alone other ties.

source_issues: 333: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to this verse. Parimelazhagar's gloss has the misprint இயல்பினையுடையப்து.
334: Manakkudavar's closing note is garbled (நிலை பா ைக றிற்று), and Parimelazhagar's gloss has several misprints.
338: Parimelazhagar spells the word குடும்பை where the verse has குடம்பை.
340: Parimelazhagar's closing remark has இவை ஏது பாட்டானும், evidently ஏழு (seven verses, 334-340).
